iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (434 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, apple’s fresh HomeView just rolled out last Friday, but some early adopters reported problems with Siri AI in their first days of use.
  • Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.
  • Per the organization’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple’s fresh HomeView just rolled out last Friday, but some early adopters reported problems with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the organization’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:.

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail.

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri concerns on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta people. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

According to recent reports, with HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new problem you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496.

In a recent development, it’s understandable that complications might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

How has Siri AI been working for you on HomeView? Let us know in the comments.

Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps.
  • The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027.
  • “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”.

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly states it has no plans for a native Mac app.

Recent findings suggest that you can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Industry observers note that planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the organization.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the tech giant behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Patch: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:.

“We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team looks. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”.

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but the early Black Friday sales are in full swing. Whether you want a full-featured fitness smartwatch or a more recovery-focused tracker, here are the discounts you can find right now, including on brands like Apple, Oura, Garmin, and more.

It has been revealed that the Oura Ring 5 is at its lowest ever price: $299 for black and silver, $399 for all other colors. But that price is particularly low right now, since the Peak membership that normally goes for $239 is now $199. Peak is the middle tier, and it's the one I recommend. This is the brand-new Apple Watch model, and it's actually worth the upgrade. Right now, I'm seeing it for as low as $329, down from the list price of $399. Oura (specifically, the Oura Ring 5).

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for a lot of commuters who want an electric scooter to get to and from work, you don’t need a tricked-out ride that costs over $1,000 and keeps up with the Porsches on the road. Something much more modest — and affordable will do the trick.

I’ve recently been testing two scooters — the Apollo Dash and the Segway E3 Go — which are made for commuters, and can be purchased for less than $600. I’ve found them to be fairly evenly matched, so to help you decide which is best for your needs, I’ve broken things down into a round-by-round comparison.

The Apollo Dash has a top speed of 22 MPH, a max range of 25 miles, and has a 600W motor and 480Wh battery.

The Segway E3 Go has a top speed of 20 MPH, a max range of 25 miles, a 400W motor, and front suspension.

The Apollo Dash is regularly priced at $699, but as of this writing, is on sale for $529 at Apollo.com; the Segway E3 Go is regularly $649, but for Black Friday, I've seen it on sale for $449.

Both of these scooters cut a pretty sleek profile. I personally like the cleaner lines of the Apollo as it transitions from the downtube to the deck; Segway’s folding mechanism, as well as its front suspension, makes things look a little busier.

Recent findings suggest that however, from a comfort standpoint, I liked the raked handlebars of the Segway over the Apollo, and the fact that the turn signal switch is located by your left thumb. By comparison, the Dash requires you to use your right thumb to activate the right turn signal, which means you have to take your thumb off the throttle.

It has been revealed that the display is one area where Segway and Apollo really differ; the E3 Go has a more traditional color LCD screen that demonstrates your speed and battery life. The Dash, on the other hand, uses a grid of white LEDs, which also shows your speed and battery life in a more basic way. However, The Apollo Dash also has a quad lock mount just below, so if you have a compatible phone case, you can use your phone as a digital dashboard.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

According to recent reports, I like the folding mechanism on both scooters; you can collapse them in mere seconds, but I'm giving the advantage here to Segway. You can simply press on a flap with your foot, so you don't have to lean down.

Sources indicate that apollo’s scooter is slightly lighter than Segway’s — 43 pounds as opposed to 46.7 pounds. You’re going to get a workout either way.

According to recent reports, one of my biggest concerns as a rider is being seen by other drivers. The Apollo’s large light bar, which extends the length of the downtube, makes you far more noticeable at night. In addition, you can adjust the angle of its headlight. By comparison, the Segway’s headlight is fixed, and it has no other lights in the front.

Both scooters have turn signals in the handlebars; however, only Apollo lets you adjust how long they remain on; from within the app, you can set a period from seven seconds or until you deactivate it.

I still wish both had turn signals in the rear of the scooter too, like the Segway Max G3 Plus or the Apollo City.

On my steep hill test (which has a max grade of 10%), the Segway slowed down to 4 MPH on the steepest section; I had to do a little wiggling of the handlebars to keep it balanced. By comparison, the Apollo managed to get up the same hill at 8 MPH — not exactly a speed record, but it was twice as fast as the Segway.

On a hill with a less steep grade of 5.7%, both scooters performed about the same, slowing to around 12 MPH.

Recent findings suggest that the raked handlebars, front suspension, and larger tires of the Segway E3 Go really made a difference, especially at speed. The scooter felt more stable when I was cruising at 20+ MPH, and was much less jarring than the suspension-less Apollo when I went over bumps and potholes.

According to recent reports, both the Apollo and Segway are rated for a max distance of 25 miles, but that’s assuming ideal conditions, and if you poke along at around 9 MPH on a flat road. With both scooters at full charge, Segway estimated that it had 11.2 miles of range, compared to 17 for the Apollo when both were set to their max performance levels. If you want to eke out a bit more range, both scooters offer regenerative braking.

I took them one at a time on an identical 5.5-mile loop around my town, going up and down the same hills. After a 5.5-mile ride, the Apollo had 55% battery left, while Segway’s had just 32%.

Now, range will vary greatly from one rider to another, but I suspect that the more powerful motor in the Apollo scooter enabled it to use power more efficiently during my test.

Both Segway’s and Apollo’s apps let you customize how the scooter performs, to a certain extent. For example, with each, you can specify the max speed for each performance setting, so if you don’t want to zoom along at 20 MPH in Sport mode, you don’t have to.

However, Apollo’s app offers a bit more customization. You can, for instance, set the amount of time that the turn signals remain on, and also fine-tune the throttle response, if you want to get off to a faster start.

According to recent reports, after testing both the Apollo Dash and the Segway E3 Go, neither really pulls away from the other to make this a decisive victory. Still, over these seven rounds, the Apollo Dash takes this matchup, winning four rounds to the Segway E3 Go’s three.

According to recent reports, I liked the design of the Segway’s handlebars and controls, and it felt more comfortable and stable while riding. And, at the time of this writing, it was $80 cheaper. However, the Apollo Dash proved more capable when scooting up hills, its lighting makes it far more visible, and it had a better range in my testing.

If you don't have hills to climb, then the Segway would be the better pick, but if you're facing some inclines, then I would lean towards the Apollo.

This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the previous post on this topic, weâve seen how the Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS) and transform (DTFT) are used to analyze infinite-duration periodic and non-periodic discrete signals. Now, itâs time to turn to realistic digital signal processing where signals are not only discrete, but also finite in duration.

Suppose we have N samples of a signal - itâs a list of N numbers:.

We want to analyze the frequencies present in this signal; in other words, to find the coefficients in a series of complex exponentials that reconstructs the signal. One option is to assume that x[n] is an infinite domain signal with zero values outside our N samples, and then compute its DTFT:.

It has been revealed that however, this is a continuous function of frequency w, so itâs difficult compute on an actual computer; we cannot evaluate and store it for all w, so we have to choose which w to compute it for. We'll soon see how this choice is made.

Sources indicate that but there's an alternative way to look at the problem. We only have N samples of the signal x, so we can assume they represent a single period of a periodic signal. And in that case, we can use DTFS; recall that the coefficients of the series are:.

In a recent development, as weâve seen in the post on the DTFS, this series can be used to reconstruct a discrete, periodic signal precisely. Since our signal x[n] is finite and we assume itâs just one period of a periodic signal, it means we can also reconstruct x[n] precisely using a DTFS.

This is the main insight behind the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). First, by convention [1] we define:.

It has been revealed that this is called the Discrete Fourier Transform of x[n]. The term transform may be a bit puzzling here - after all, weâre just using the series coefficients - so isnât it more proper to just say series? Perhaps, though in mathematics a transform has a pretty general meaning of "a mapping that takes a mathematical object and produces another object"; in that sense, "transform" is proper here because we take an object - x[n] and produce another object - X[k].

Moreover, DFT and DTFT are intimately related. Recall how we stated earlier that the DTFT is tricky to compute because w is a continuous variable? Well, the DFT gives us a way to sample that variable into the discrete domain:.

So the DFT can be seen as exactly N equally spaced samples of the DTFT.

Since the goal of this post is specifically to demonstrate computable methods of applying Fourier analysis to discrete digital signals, hereâs the Python code to calculate the DFT of a signal:.

It shouldnât be hard to see the correspondence between this code and the mathematical formula for X[k]. Pythonâs Numpy code is vectorized by default, so the weights array is computed in whole for every k (because n is an array of indices [0..N-1]).

In my earlier post on the complex roots of unity, weâve seen how powers of the roots of unity form an orthogonal basis for \mathbb{C}^n. Now letâs show the beautiful theoretical connection between this fact and the DFT.

Recall that the N-th roots of unity can be written as:.

Since all z_k are just powers of w=z_1=e^{i2\pi/N}, we can write them as:.

The conjugates of the roots of unity are roots of unity themselves:.

With z_k^* being the same as z_{N-k}, so when we enumerate all the roots of unity, weâre also enumerating their conjugates, just in a reversed order.

With that in mind, letâs denote [2] \omega=z_1^*=e^{-i2\pi/N}, and examine the sequence:.

The vectors formed by (element-wise) raising \mu_N to integer powers from 0 to N-1 can be collected into a matrix:.

In the roots of unity post, weâve proven that the rows of this matrix form an orthogonal basis over \mathbb{C}^N. In other words, any vector in \mathbb{C}^N can be represented as a linear combination of the rows of F.

I hope you can see where this is going! Letâs consider the signal x[n] as a column vector in \mathbb{C}^N. The DFT of x can be computed by multiplying x by the matrix F:.

According to recent reports, take a minute to convince yourself this is true, by working through the multiplication for a specific row k, e.g. X[2] is computed via row-column multiplication the third row (counting from 0) of F and x[n].

According to recent reports, our F is called the Fourier Matrix or the DFT Matrix. Previously weâve seen Python code that directly computes the DFT; hereâs a version that does this via the matrix multiplication approach:.

Sources indicate that more than the computational convenience though, thereâs theoretical elegance here. Back when we were discussing the continuous Fourier series, weâve seen how the trigonometric functions (or - equivalently - complex exponentials) form an orthogonal basis for square integrable functions.

Here, we see a similar linear algebra connection in discrete time - the vectors formed from powers of complex roots of unity form an orthogonal basis in \mathbb{C}^N and can thus be used to represent any sequence of N complex values.

Which brings us to the next topic: reconstructing a signal from its DFT representation.

Industry observers note that there are two equivalent approaches to find the inverse DFT - the formula we can use to reconstruct x[n] given X[k]. The first approach is going back to DTFS, where the reconstruction formula is:.

According to recent reports, recall that our convention is X[k]=Na_k. Therefore:.

This is the Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform formula.

Letâs examine the other approach now, because it uses our linear algebra interpretation in an enlightening way.

It has been revealed that recall the Fourier matrix F, and consider F_c - the same matrix where every element is the conjugate of the corresponding element of F. If:.

What happens if we multiply F by F_c?

We have seen in the roots of unity post that this amounts to:.

Where I is the identity matrix. Since F is a square matrix, any matrix that multiplies with it to give the identity is its inverse:.

Which is the same reconstruction formula we obtained from the DTFS. In mathematics, itâs always a good sign when we obtain the same result using different methods!

The linear algebra interpretation here is clear: the vectors formed by the powers of roots of unity form an orthogonal basis over \mathbb{C}^N. Therefore, every vector x\in\mathbb{C}^N can be represented as a linear combination of these vectors. Moreover, this transformation is invertible, and the original vector can be reconstructed by left-multiplying its DFT vector X by F^{-1}.

Itâs time for a fully worked example; the entire Python code for this example is available on GitHub; read through its main function, which is well commented.

Recall the sampled triangular signal weâve used in the previous post; here, letâs use a single cycle:.

In code, this is just an array of numbers:.

Calculating the DFT of this signal using the code shown earlier produces the following values; remember that X[k] consists of complex numbers, so we represent them as a magnitude-phase pair. Phase is only shown for nonzero coefficients, because the phase of zero is undefined [3]:.

Obviously, weâd get exactly the same numbers by using the matrix multiplication method of computing the DFT. And to reconstruct the signal, we multiply by the computed IDFT matrix to get the original signal back. The reconstruction matches the original signal precisely, with any differences being attributable to floating point round-off.

The sample code contains another method of computing the DFT of this signal - by calling NumPyâs fft.fft function. This refers to the Fast Fourier Transform, which is considered to be one of the most important algorithms of the 20th century. By exploiting the structure of the Fourier matrix F, FFT computes the product F\cdot x in O(N \log N) operations, compared with O(N^2) for direct matrix-vector multiplication. I plan to cover how this works in a future post.

Looking carefully at the signal used in the Example section above, we see that itâs actually one full cycle out of a sampled triangle wave. This is convenient, because repeating the block reproduces the original triangle wave. But what happens when the samples cover only part of the cycle?

Take for example just the first 10 samples of the triangle wave:.

If we naively extend this signal periodically, things wonât line up (there will be a jump at the end of every cycle). We can still calculate its DFT, of course; these are the coefficients weâll get:.

Sources indicate that while the coefficients still come in conjugate pairs (because the samples are real), the original triangleâs frequencies no longer coincide with the DFTâs frequency bins, so their contributions spread across multiple bins. This is called spectral leakage.

Industry observers note that by applying the IDFT we can still reconstruct the original 10-sample signal perfectly! So if all we need is reconstruction, spectral leakage isnât an problem; but if weâre doing frequency analysis, it skews the situation somewhat, adding frequencies that didnât really exist in the underlying triangle wave - just to account for the discontinuity. In real-world signal processing, such issues are usually addressed by applying special window functions to the signal after sampling - these help alleviate leakage by tapering the signal close to zero at the edges.

iPadOS 27.3 is now in beta and will launch to all customers next month, here are three new features it introduces for iPad.

There’s a new setting in iPadOS 27.3 that I instantly turned on and have been loving. It lets you double-tap the top of a window to resize it.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if ‘Windowed Apps’ is enabled there’s now a fresh toggle: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom.’.

In a recent development, I’ve been using this gesture all the time in the beta, because it lets me resize my window to fullscreen then revert it to its previous size with ease. It’s an intuitive, convenient way to resize windows for different tasks.

Read more: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on.

Visual intelligence was available on iPad already, but iPadOS 27.3 adds a dedicated hub for using the feature: a fresh Siri mode in the Camera app.

According to recent reports, iOS 27 brought Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app, but it was missing from iPad. iPadOS 27.3 corrects that oversight, letting you use your iPad’s built-in Camera app to ask Siri about any object you capture.

Sources indicate that baking visual intelligence into Camera should expose the feature to a lot more iPad users, since before you had to set up a custom control or shortcut for it. And with how much better visual intelligence has gotten thanks to Siri AI, the Siri mode is a valuable addition.

Read more: iOS 27 gives the Camera app on iPhone a brand new mode.

Freeform is gaining a variety of upcoming features in iPadOS 27.3. They’re available in macOS and iOS too, but out of all Apple platforms, Freeform feels very much built for the iPad.

These are the best over-ear headphones I tested in 2025 (or ever, really). Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $348 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever during the early Black Friday sale from Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that the XM6 headphones improve on what were already excellent headphones. Sony upped the count of microphones from eight to 12 when compared to the XM5, which improves more than just how well you sound to someone on a phone call. The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly. If you switch from a noisy room to a quiet one, the XM6 can switch from ANC to "aware mode" (if you have Adaptive Sound Control on).

These headphones have a lot more features that you can nerd out on in their companion app. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. I really like being able to see what codec you're listening to in the app's main menu. That way, there's no guessing if you're getting the best audio quality or not. They will give you 30 hours of battery life with ANC on and 40 hours of juice with ANC off. There's an AUX (3.5mm) jack for wired listening, which is a nice touch for audiophiles who still rock iPod Classics (or is that just me?).

The XM6s were not just the best headphones of 2025, but are still the best ones of 2026 and likely to be the best ones for years to come. For $348, you'll be securing the best for a record-low price.

When I think about Adam Driver as an actor, two words come to mind: stoic and intense. I see a disciplined actor with no social media presence who lets his work speak for itself.

Part of that discipline comes from his military background, while the rest stems from his time at Juilliard. Driver would have loved to come up in the 1960s and 1970s, as he feels cut from the same cloth as Robert De Niro and Al Pacino.

It has been revealed that right now, Driver stars in “Paper Tiger,” James Gray’s Latest York City crime drama about two brothers whose business dealings become entangled with the Russian mob. Driver has received rave reviews for his performance, with some critics calling it the actor’s best work. In honor of “Paper Tiger,” here are Driver's five best movies.

The irony of Driver’s career is that despite being known for his intensity, he’s extremely funny. Driver’s breakout role came as Adam Sackler in the HBO comedy “Girls.” Since this list concerns movies, I’ll select another project from that era: “What If,” or in some territories, “The F Word.” (“What If” is a better title, for what it’s worth.) One night, Wallace (Daniel Radcliffe) and Chantry (Zoe Kazan) meet and hit it off. Although Chantry has a boyfriend, Wallace elects to be her friend because he’s in love with her.

Sources indicate that wallace and Chantry seem perfect for each other, but bad timing and unfortunate circumstances keep them apart. Driver plays Allan, Wallace’s best friend. Allan is a boisterous friend who encourages Wallace to tell Chantry how he feels. “What If” is a charming rom-com with a hilarious performance from Driver, who deserves recognition for his line delivery in the “greatest moment of my life” speech.

In a recent development, like many “Star Wars” fans, I have problems with the sequel trilogy. My biggest gripe is with “The Rise of Skywalker,” especially the entire Palpatine debacle. It’s difficult to tell the story of Driver’s career without a “Star Wars” movie, so I’ll go with “The Force Awakens,” the highly entertaining popcorn blockbuster that kicked off Lucasfilm’s Disney era. Thirty years after the events of “Return of the Jedi,” the galaxy faces a latest Imperial threat: the First Order.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Recent findings suggest that the Resistance, led by General Leia Organa (Carrie Fisher), recruits a fresh set of rebels, including Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), Finn (John Boyega), and Rey (Daisy Ridley). Driver plays Kylo Ren, a ruthless warrior in the First Order out to find the location of Luke Skywalker. Driver’s intensity translates seamlessly to a villainous role. Kylo is Gen Z’s version of Darth Vader. Driver plays Ren as a brooding, sad boy with daddy complications. It’s a subversion of masculinity and an interesting addition to the “Star Wars” lineup of iconic villains.

In a recent development, spike Lee remarked it best. While speaking with BBC Radio 1 for “BlacKkKlansman,” Lee described Driver as a “beast.” Lee went on to praise Driver’s range as an actor. No arguments here, Mr. Lee. In “BlacKkKlansman,” John David Washington stars as Ron Stallworth, the first Black detective in the Colorado Springs Police Department.

Looking to infiltrate the local Ku Klux Klan, Ron poses as a white supremacist over the phone. The Klan buys it and wants to meet Ron. Since he’s Black, Ron recruits his white Jewish co-worker, Flip Zimmerman (Driver), to pose as him. The ruse works, and the duo infiltrates the Ku Klux Klan to thwart its nefarious plans. “BlacKkKlansman” is a witty and sharp critique of racism and extremist political movements.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also a film that eerily resembles events from the current day, which is scary in itself. Driver’s grounded presence is the perfect counterbalance to Washington’s excessive charisma. Driver earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor, the first of his career.

I enjoy Driver as a heel. He knows how to get under my skin as a villain. He did it in “Star Wars,” and he arguably did it better in “The Last Duel.” Ridley Scott’s period piece is based on the last trial by combat in medieval France. The movie is split into three parts, detailing the viewpoints of Jean de Carrouges (Matt Damon), Jacques le Gris (Driver), and Marguerite de Carrouges (Jodie Comer).

Marguerite accuses Jacques of rape while Jean is out of town. With no physical evidence, it becomes Marguerite’s word versus Jacques’s, with the latter vehemently denying the accusation. Believing he must defend his family's honor, Jean requests a duel to the death, which Jacques accepts.

Don’t let the box office failures turn you away from this excellent drama and Scott’s best movie this decade. It’s a shockingly violent movie, but also one that rewards patience. It’s not good vs. bad. Instead, it’s about morally complex characters, making for a far more interesting dilemma.

According to recent reports, if I were having trouble in a relationship, “Marriage Story” might be at the bottom of the pile of films to watch. Noah Baumbach’s drama about a couple going through a divorce features some of the meanest, rawest, and most emotional scenes I’ve ever seen. At times, it punches you in the heart and makes you question everything you knew about love. At the center of the movie are Charlie (Driver) and Nicole Barber (Scarlett Johansson), a married couple.

Recent findings suggest that charlie, a theater director, and Nicole, an actress, agree to a divorce. Charlie remains in Fresh York, while Nicole heads to Los Angeles with their son, Henry (Azhy Robertson). The couple begins divorce proceedings cordially, but when lawyers get involved, it becomes cutthroat. Some of these scenes between Charlie and Nicole, especially the climactic argument, are like watching a car crash — you can’t look away. It’s an acting tour de force for Driver and Johansson, who earned their respective Oscar nominations.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a newly introduced setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

In a recent development, while wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the newly introduced slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Latest Update: Agentics: Mushy Software

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 12gramsofcarbon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A lot of software is ‘glue code’ — a little bit of logic that connects service A to service B, often an interface or class that maps from one field to another.
  • In 2026, glue is not the only way to connect two services.
  • Sources indicate that agent layers inside and around a traditional software stack make any application feel moldable and mushy, if you have access to the internals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A lot of software is ‘glue code’ — a little bit of logic that connects service A to service B, often an interface or class that maps from one field to another. I like the ‘glue’ metaphor a lot. Glue starts fluid, but swiftly sets in place. It becomes brittle. If you bend the interface in the wrong way, the glue will snap and break.

In 2026, glue is not the only way to connect two services. You can also now use an agent or an LLM.1 The agent is inherently flexible. It can write code on the fly, so it can bend when schemas change. We’ve taken to calling this ‘agent grease.’2 Glue code makes things stick. Pour some agent grease in the joints and watch the whole thing start humming along again.

Sources indicate that agent layers inside and around a traditional software stack make any application feel moldable and mushy, if you have access to the internals. Any software can be any other software. Want to turn that dashboard into Pac-Man? Sure, why not. Coupling has always been a problem; in agent world, strict coupling is both undesirable and maybe impossible.

I think Claude Artifacts are probably the most well used example of mushy software. These things are fully functional applications, but they are also infinitely moldable. Using agents is an expected part of the interaction pattern. The application itself is almost purposely half baked, because the end user is supposed to use an agent to craft / finish the rest.

Mushy software has tradeoffs from traditional, hard software.

Sources indicate that mushy software is much slower. Flexibility always comes at the cost of speed. ASICs are faster than GPUs are faster than CPUs. If you have an agent in the loop, anything you do may take multiple high latency inference calls.

According to recent reports, mushy software is much harder to reason about. Well made software is modular and does one thing. There is a clear interface. Mushy software has no contract, no obvious interface. Or, put a different way, the whole thing is the interface. So you have to have some sense of what the internals do, in order to make it all work consistently.

Sources indicate that you (the builder) have way less control over how people choose to use your software. You can’t easily create a happy path, nor can you hide warts. In some sense, that’s the whole point!

I think a good analogy to all this is the SpaceX raptor engine, shown in different iterations below.

Or maybe a breadboard vs a finished circuit.

According to recent reports, at Nori we’ve been experimenting a lot with mushy software. All of our internal tools are covered in agent grease. Normally, the way this works is we assign a single long running PM agent to be the directly responsible agent for each tool. That PM farms tasks out to subworkers, while keeping its main thread relatively clean. It builds the whole thing in an isolated git repo and vpc, and throws it up on AWS. It keeps track of bugs and errors, live. If anything ever goes wrong, it is self healing — that is, it will automatically try and fix itself and then retry whatever thing broke. You can read more about our PM agent architecture here:.

Sources indicate that the internal tools are never really done. They are mushy. The PM agent sticks around, persistent, resumable, with its own project state. It has visibility over the database and all of the code that makes up the internal tool. Any time you want to make a change, just lob the ask over to the PM. The whole app can transform on a dime. And some of our internal tools can call out to agents themselves, which adds another layer of grease. I have a draft post on how we handle our content syndication that will hopefully come out soon, but the tldr is that any post on substack instantly becomes an X article and a YouTube video and a LinkedIn post, which then turn into reels and pull quotes and so on.

This has been so powerful that I increasingly think all internal tools should be mushy.

Industry observers note that we’ve also been experimenting with how to ship mushy software. What if you could let any client dynamically revision their SaaS on the fly? How could we make that effective and safe and useful?

You may think that the cube mode is a joke, but no, that’s actually how I use agents these days.

One last thought, related to the above. I recently said that we should be having more fun when building with AI:.

Recent findings suggest that [Because AI is primarily used for work] it has become drab, and boring, and buttoned up. People used to do crazy weird AI body horror glitch art, and now it’s all just this guy.

Industry observers note that that’s not how it should be. These things are so weird. And they like building things, and they will build anything.

In a recent development, software used to be a really serious endeavor because making most software was hard work, and required a lot of sustained effort. Now that software is cheap, it has permission to be fun and childlike. Sometimes I worry that we’re so wrapped in AI doomerism and tokenmaxxing and trying to show off for our various status-y groups that we forget to actually play with these incredible toys.

The best thing about mushy software is that you can just be like, ‘make my chats a rotating psychedelic cube’, and the agents will do that, and it’s hilarious! Make more things mushy!

If you want to see more of our mushy software, follow Jiro (our internal Nori agent) on Twitter or me on substack or join our Agentics community slack.

Industry observers note that agentics is the study of how to use and reason about agents. Learn more about how to use agents at our agent learning hub.

According to recent reports, if you want AI employees, we can help! Nori is a platform to build and deploy AI employees. Check out noriagentic.com for more.

I’m using these mostly interchangeably, but in most cases I mean ‘agent’ as in ‘Claude Code’ or ‘Codex’ and not a one-off LLM call.

we actually call it agent lube but that seemed weirder so im leaving this note in the footnotes for all the weird people who read footnotes.

I drove the Audi Q3 and Mini Countryman for a week — here’s the sub-$52K crossover I’d buy with my own money

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I think about luxury vehicles, the first things that instantly come to mind are $60,000+ price tags.
  • Recent findings suggest that each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory.
  • With an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I think about luxury vehicles, the first things that instantly come to mind are $60,000+ price tags. Thankfully, entry-level luxury crossovers exist, and they’re some of the smartest buys on the market. For my next comparison, I’m pitting the Mini Countryman and Audi Q3 against each other in a head-to-head matchup to see which compact crossover is worth buying.

Recent findings suggest that each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory. It’s actually been years since I last tested a Mini — the electric Countryman EV — so you can imagine how eager I was to get back into the gas-powered 2027 Mini Countryman S All4.

With an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin. I will say, however, that you can’t dismiss the Q3 just yet, because after a week’s worth of driving, it too impressed me on plenty of occasions.

2.0L TFSI turbocharged I4 Engine.

2.0-Liter MINI TwinPower Turbo Inline 4-Cylinder Engine.

22 mpg city / 29 mpg highway / 25 mpg combined.

24 mpg city / 32 mpg highway / 27 mpg combined.

Frankly, this one’s tough because these compact crossovers cater to completely different tastes, so personal preference heavily influences the decision.

The 2026 Audi Q3 leans heavily into conventional luxury aesthetics, dressed in Malpelo Blue Metallic with the Black Optic package — which shimmers in the light. Alongside the sharp LED headlights up front and OLED taillights in the back, the package makes it look sleek and unmistakably upscale.

By contrast, the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 embraces a sportier edge and distinctive British flair. It’s undeniably boxier and more upright, yet it’s loaded with personality — I especially love its Slate Blue Metallic paint job with a contrasting black roof and stripes. Even its LED lighting features customizable light signatures to match its charming looks.

Ultimately, it comes down to whether you prefer understated German luxury or retro-modern charm — making this category an easy tie.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Best short distance fuel economy.

Best long distance fuel economy.

Looking at their spec sheets, it’s quite clear that the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 holds a slight advantage in terms of fuel economy with an EPA-estimated 27 mpg combined (24 city / 32 highway), compared to the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro’s 25 mpg combined rating (22 city / 29 highway).

In a recent development, in my real-world testing, however, that gap turned into a surprisingly wide canyon. Over 313.6 miles of mixed driving in the Countryman, I averaged an impressive 31.1 mpg overall — easily exceeding its EPA estimate. Better yet, it hit 30.5 mpg on my best short-distance trip and soared to 36.1 mpg on a longer highway stretch.

In a recent development, in contrast, the Audi Q3 struggled to match its window sticker across 243.5 miles of testing, averaging just 23.2 mpg overall. Even on my best long-distance (26.5 mpg) run, it never came close to its 29 mpg highway rating.

If keeping fuel costs low is a top priority, the Mini is the clear standout here, saving you noticeably more at the pump in the long run.

Most compact crossovers prioritize fuel economy and put driving dynamics in the back seat, but not these two. Better yet, I love how both prove you don’t need a massive engine to have fun behind the wheel.

The 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 is my favorite of the two by a narrow margin, packing a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four engine that puts out 241 horsepower and 295 lb-ft of torque. The Audi similarly has impressive muscle under the hood: a 2.0-liter TFSI four-cylinder that delivers 255 horsepower and 273 lb-ft of torque.

According to recent reports, what I will say after being behind the wheel of both is that they’re noticeably zippy off the line, with speedy acceleration that makes it effortless to overtake at cruising speed. While the Q3’s powertrain actually surprised me with a smooth delivery that almost makes it feel more like an EV, it doesn’t beat the Countryman when the road starts to curve. The Mini's lower, wider stance keeps it feeling noticeably more planted through corners, preserving that signature go-kart agility it’s known for.

Industry observers note that despite their smaller footprints, these compact crossovers still offer plenty of room to make lengthy road trips a breeze. However, the 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 holds a slight advantage. That’s because it offers 40.4 inches of front legroom and 37 inches in the rear, which beats the 2026 Audi Q3’s 40 inches up front and 36.1 inches in the back. Additionally, they deliver nearly identical trunk space around 25 cubic feet, easily accommodating my electric scooter.

Sources indicate that inside, they take very different approaches to cabin materials. The Audi leans into traditional luxury with genuine leather seating surfaces, wood inlays, and solid soundproofing that keeps road noise at a minimum. Obviously, the higher price of the Q3 is justified by its more luxurious aesthetics.

Industry observers note that mini takes a totally different approach that gives it a charming style that feels genuinely original. It trades classic leather for Vescin leather-free upholstery and knitted textile surfaces on the dash and doors — which I have to say looked funky and stylish at first glance, but they eventually grew on me.

Sources indicate that sure, the Audi comes up a smidge short on rear legroom, but the Q3 just feels noticeably more plush over long stretches. And when I factor in Audi’s smoother, more intuitive adaptive cruise assist on highways, the Q3 edges ahead as the more relaxing cruiser.

Audi needs to prove it’s worth spending about $7,500 more over its rival. But does it?

While the 2026 Audi Q3 doesn’t skimp on luxury amenities, it simply makes you pay noticeably more for them. Even so, I appreciate its crisp 360-degree camera coverage, head-up display that projects driving details onto the windshield to lessen distractions, and seamless Park Assist Plus for automatic parking. Inside, its panoramic sunroof and vibrant LED ambient lighting create a more upscale look at night — while its large blind-spot warning lights mounted right on the side mirrors are impossible to miss in heavy traffic or in the daytime.

However, you’re still getting better value for the money out of the Mini Countryman S ALL4. For starters, its circular 9.4-inch OLED touchscreen display is a sight to behold and runs a far more intuitive interface. Although it ditches the traditional driver’s cluster entirely, the flip-up head-up display keeps distractions at a minimum. I’m also significant on sound, and the punchy Harman Kardon surround sound system easily outclasses the Audi's Sonos setup.

Not only does it offer full 360-degree camera coverage, but it also includes a clever Backup Assistant that takes over the wheel and automatically retraces the path I took to get into the spot. And finally, I really love the adaptive LED headlights with customizable light signatures and cornering lights.

When I weigh this robust feature set against that $7,540 price gap, the Mini delivers far more bang for your buck.

According to recent reports, let me finish by saying that I’d gladly buy either compact crossover in a heartbeat with my own money. That mentioned, the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro does come up short once the tallies are counted.

It has been revealed that if you prioritize traditional luxury materials, a quieter cabin, and a smoother adaptive cruise control system for long highway commutes, it remains an immensely likable daily driver that costs less than the average luxury vehicle. Honestly, despite losing this head-to-head matchup, I would still gladly buy the Audi Q3 — it’s just that the Mini Countryman gives you more for less.

It has been revealed that the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 emerges as the clear winner, and it’s the one I’d ultimately pick. Between its punchy driving dynamics, standout real-world fuel economy, sharper OLED infotainment system, and $7,540 price advantage in this comparison, it simply delivers too much personality and value to ignore.

#62607. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3335 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • According to recent reports, the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

According to recent reports, the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Recent findings suggest that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

Sources indicate that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

In a recent development, druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

In a recent development, an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

Industry observers note that he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs indicates the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

It has been revealed that to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most notable processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

It has been revealed that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she states, of solar eclipse photography.

According to recent reports, the European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

According to recent reports, when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Sources indicate that habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

Industry observers note that the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” states Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

It has been revealed that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller indicates. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

In a recent development, “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

In a recent development, if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller indicates with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

In a recent development, but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” notes Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

It has been revealed that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Recent findings suggest that among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

According to recent reports, those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Recent findings suggest that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

Recent findings suggest that “Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” notes Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

Industry observers note that for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

It has been revealed that druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as rapidly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

Recent findings suggest that the crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

According to recent reports, “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller indicates. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

It was part of the original pitch, and to finally get there—everything, when you’re pitching a show, it all feels like a pipe dream,” said Lyle. “You don’t think you’re actually going to be able to do any of this, especially something that you know is only gonna be if you get a first season, a second season, a third season. #62602. Breaking: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory
