⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing?
  • The Open Social Web Alliance aims to provide the answers.
  • In a recent development, A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing?

The Open Social Web Alliance aims to provide the answers.

In a recent development, A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on.

In a recent development, the year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide.

Recent findings suggest that A critical mass of consumers in Europe has turned its back on the platform monopolies and created a free market built on interoperable infrastructure. Today, users decide for themselves which content, which algorithms and which applications they want to use. Closed platforms have become open networks. On the ActivityPub and AT Protocol protocols (as well as Matrix for direct messaging), an ecosystem of non-commercial, public service and commercial offerings has emerged. They enrich and complement public-interest projects such as Mastodon and Eurosky, and they communicate with one another through shared interfaces.

This vision describes the Open Social Web (OSW): a decentralised, public-interest infrastructure for digital communication, based on open standards and interoperable protocols.

In a recent development, the idea of an Open Social Web is not upcoming. The Fediverse has been in development since 2008 and is home to diverse, vibrant communities that build individual applications and run instances. While its focus has so far been on Europe, North America and Japan, there are now more than 100 applications, such as Mastodon, Loops and PeerTube, and more than 42,000 active instances worldwide. Even so, the number of active owners, around 13 million, is growing only slowly. The ATmosphere community has been developing since 2022, primarily in North America but increasingly in Europe and beyond. It currently has around 43 million registered accounts and dozens of implementations and applications, such as Eurosky’s Mu, Gander and Sill.

Sources indicate that for many reasons, both protocol-based social networks are attractive alternatives to the platform economy dominated by Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet. So why have people been so hesitant to switch?

Recent findings suggest that we have identified five key challenges: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. Below, we set out how we can overcome them and make the Open Social Web Alliance a shared success.

Sources indicate that an ecosystem like this does not emerge on its own. Our roadmap demonstrates how the Open Social Web could reach a relevant scale within just a few months. It takes political will, smart regulation, sufficient funding and a broad coalition of actors willing to share responsibility. The task is massive. But the levers are there.

As a first step, we are founding the Open Social Web Alliance: an open alliance of stakeholders from civil society, research, business, media, culture and the public sector who are committed to the shared governance of the OSW. It brings together a wide range of existing communities and initiatives and is to be supported in future by a publicly funded secretariat. Its central goal: building and operating the OSW’s core infrastructure (see Section 2.1, Infrastructure).

Our roadmap envisions that the German federal government will explicitly support the Alliance, for instance by acting as patron of an Open Social Web Summit in autumn 2026, to which everyone with an interest in the OSW would be invited.

At the summit, the Alliance would adopt its charter, setting out how it admits upcoming members and how it intends to implement its governance going forward (see Section 2.2, Governance). By spring 2027, public funding for the infrastructure would be in place, along with a first core funding round of public and private capital for innovation and applications (see Section 2.3, Funding). The Alliance would publish its first Social Web Health Report, featuring findings from user surveys, legal, technical and academic analyses, and clear recommendations for further development (see Section 2.4, Appeal). In parallel, the federal and state governments would ensure that the legal basis for cooperation between public service media, other media, business and civil society is established (see Section 2.5, Public Mandate). The federal government would also champion the OSW idea at EU level, for instance through an implementation push for effective digital legislation. As key stakeholders such as the federal government adopt OSW applications as their primary channel of communication, influential creators and publishers would follow suit, and central political debates would quickly shift to the Open Social Web. Taken together, these measures would reduce the influence and appeal of today’s dominant Massive Tech platforms.

The Open Social Web Alliance is looking for allies: people and organisations who are convinced that genuine social networks can create real value.

We look forward to hearing from you. Got better ideas than ours? Even better!

What’s Going on with The Trade Desk Stock? 3 Reasons Investors Are Losing Confidence.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Trade Desk (TTD -8.10%) used to be one of the market's favorite advertising technology companies.
  • It has been revealed that but the sentiment has changed.
  • The problem is not that digital advertising is going away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lawrence Nga – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:11AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than The Trade Desk ›.

Recent findings suggest that the Trade Desk (TTD -8.10%) used to be one of the market's favorite advertising technology companies. It offered investors an attractive way to benefit from the shift toward digital advertising, particularly as more people watched television through streaming services.

It has been revealed that but the sentiment has changed. The stock has fallen sharply as investors question whether the manufacturer can maintain its growth, compete with technology giants, and protect its profits.

The problem is not that digital advertising is going away. It is that The Trade Desk is struggling to turn the industry's growth into growth for its own business.

I see three main reasons behind the market's pessimism.

The biggest concern is the company's slowing revenue. In the third quarter of 2026, The Trade Desk generated $736 million in revenue, down 0.5% from a year earlier. That is a sharp reversal from the 18% growth it recorded in the same quarter last year.

According to recent reports, the slowdown is not limited to one quarter. Revenue increased just 4% during the first nine months of 2026 compared with 20% growth over the same period in 2025. For a tech giant that investors once expected to grow rapidly, these numbers are difficult to ignore.

Industry observers note that to understand why this matters, consider what The Trade Desk actually does. It provides software that helps advertisers buy digital advertising across websites, apps, and streaming services. Instead of negotiating separately with hundreds of publishers, advertisers can use its platform to plan and manage campaigns in one place.

In a recent development, the opportunity should be substantial. More advertising dollars are moving online, and streaming services are creating new places for advertisers to reach consumers. Yet The Trade Desk is not capturing that opportunity as promptly as investors expected.

Industry observers note that management is investing in artificial intelligence (AI) and improving its advertising platform to help customers run more effective campaigns. Its expanded relationship with Netflix is another positive development.

But latest products and partnerships are only valuable if they increase advertising spending. Investors want to see customers putting more money through the platform, not simply that the organization is launching new technology or entering into partnerships.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

The second concern is competition, particularly from Amazon, Google, and Meta.

The Trade Desk built its business around an independent platform that helps advertisers buy advertising across the open internet. Its value proposition is that advertisers can access different publishers and advertising inventory through one platform, rather than relying entirely on the advertising ecosystems of individual technology companies.

In a recent development, that independence remains valuable. But the competitive environment is changing.

Sources indicate that amazon has a particularly strong advantage. Its advertising business combines inventory with valuable shopping and purchase-intent data. Advertisers can reach consumers and measure whether campaigns lead to sales. Google and Meta also have extensive first-party data, large advertising ecosystems, and sophisticated targeting capabilities. These platforms offer something The Trade Desk cannot fully replicate: direct access to their own owners, data, and inventory.

There is also a customer relationship problem. The Trade Desk has faced tensions with major advertising agencies, including the European giant Publicis, after disagreements over its platform and commercial practices. The dispute has largely been resolved. Still, it demonstrates the bargaining power that large customers have over the organization.

It has been revealed that the risk is not necessarily that advertisers will abandon The Trade Desk overnight. Its independent position and broad relationships with publishers still serve an vital purpose. The bigger concern is that it may become harder to win incremental advertising budgets when competing platforms offer simpler, more integrated solutions.

It has been revealed that slower growth would be easier to tolerate if profits remained resilient. Unfortunately, that has not been the case.

According to recent reports, in the third quarter, adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) fell 16% year over year to $266 million. Its adjusted EBITDA margin contracted from 43% to 36%. Operating expenses increased to $643 million, compared with $578 million a year earlier, despite lower revenue.

Sources indicate that this is a difficult combination for investors. The Trade Desk historically benefited from operating leverage: as revenue grew, the company could increase profits without raising costs at the same rate. That advantage is now under pressure.

In a recent development, management has responded by restructuring, reducing its workforce by approximately 15%. That may help restore margins. But cutting costs is not a substitute for revenue growth. If the firm has to shrink its workforce simply to protect profitability, investors may question whether its previous growth model remains intact.

According to recent reports, the Trade Desk is not necessarily a broken business. It still has a substantial cash position, strong customer retention, and exposure to the long-term growth of programmatic advertising.

But the challenges are real and substantial, and investors want to see proof that the company can turn around its operations.

Sources indicate that the next few quarters will be important. Revenue growth must recover, margins must stabilize, and existing advertisers must demonstrate willingness to spend more through the platform.

Until then, The Trade Desk likely remains a problem child for investors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that demonstrates up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

“Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

In the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

According to recent reports, it’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

Sources indicate that the Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

Sources indicate that lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

  • This shift changes how devices are designed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Recent findings suggest that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026.

It has been revealed that palmer Luckey says the US government will not let Ukraine use Starshield, because it fears Russia would destroy it. Starshield is the Pentagon’s military satellite network, and SpaceX helps run it. The Anduril founder made the case to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The Latest York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

“The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey said.

He was defending Elon Musk, who spoke later that day and accused Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield speed limits. Luckey said he likes Musk personally, so people should take his view “with a pound of salt”.

His argument ran like this. Russia has hinted that it could destroy the civilian Starlink network if Ukraine keeps using it for attacks. The same satellites that cover Ukraine also orbit over the US. So Musk should not have to risk his whole network when Washington will not risk its own, Luckey said.

Recent findings suggest that “Nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win. They just want them to not lose for as long as possible, which is a bizarre and absurd warfighting position,” he said.

It has been revealed that luckey remarked he fully supports Ukraine, and that Anduril has worked there since the second day of the war. Who America sells weapons to is not his call, he added.

“I’m a dog on a chain and I need to be kept that way,” Luckey mentioned.

According to recent reports, luckey co-leads Project Meridian, the Pentagon’s 120-day study of future war, with Musk and Newt Gingrich. He noted it looks at what war could look like in 2050, and that the MITRE Corporation runs it. The group met at Cheyenne Mountain the day before. It agreed to focus on ideas that have no champion in the Pentagon.

One example is weather control, he said, such as changing where rain falls at sea so forces get a clearer view of targets. He also took credit for pushing the Trump administration to rename the Defense Department the Department of War.

Recent findings suggest that sorkin read him a criticism from Wes Bryant, who until last year ran the Pentagon’s assessment of civilian harm. Bryant called Meridian a sign of oligarchy in government. Luckey noted more than 20 people sit on it, including retired generals and admirals. Nobody attacked Eric Schmidt for joining the Defense Innovation Board under Joe Biden, he said, and the report will be public.

In a recent development, luckey wants the US to resume nuclear testing, mainly to see what an electromagnetic pulse does to modern electronics. The models used today were built for transistors thousands of times larger than those in a phone, he said. He is not confident his own systems would survive, even when built to the hardening rules.

“They were designed for the type of cell phone that Abraham Lincoln would have used,” he remarked.

He said no AI model can be controlled, because every major model has been jailbroken within months. Data centres can still be shut off, he added. The AI in weapons is a different technology from chatbots, he argued, and more reliable than the older seekers it replaces.

“I am way more afraid of the civilian collateral side for dumb weapons than I am for smart weapons,” Luckey said.

It has been revealed that some companies have used chatbots for targeting and made mistakes, he noted, without naming them. China wants Jensen Huang out of Nvidia, he said, so he wants him back. Luckey still opposes selling chips to China.

Sources indicate that luckey also defended public executions. The state should rarely use the death penalty, he said. When it does, it should do so in public and without medical cover, so people can judge whether it got it right.

According to recent reports, “Executions should be brutal. They should be violent,” he noted.

Industry observers note that he closed on his 2017 firing from Facebook, after he gave $9,000 to a pro-Trump group. He blames former Oculus colleagues, not Mark Zuckerberg, and now works with Meta on a combat headset for the US Army.

“It’s probably better for everybody that I got fired, but I have not let it go,” Luckey said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

Industry observers note that airPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

The case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:.

Recent findings suggest that the key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

It has been revealed that if you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice ….

Sources indicate that airPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

In a recent development, I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

If you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $179. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

Finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that this year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

According to recent reports, airPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

If you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

  • Sources indicate that still, it's not the key metric that really matters, because this is a war likely to be won by a different and even more critical metric.
  • It's important to be clear about this number.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lee Samaha – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:12AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Tesla ›.

Recent findings suggest that J.P. Morgan analyst Rajat Gupta believes that Tesla's (TSLA -7.64%) robotaxi fleet could match Alphabet's (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%) Waymo fleet in cumulative autonomous miles by the end of 2027. Such an event would mark a milestone in Tesla's robotaxi development.

Sources indicate that still, it's not the key metric that really matters, because this is a war likely to be won by a different and even more critical metric. It's such a key number that it will arguably determine Tesla's overall value.

It's important to be clear about this number. Going back to the We, Robot event in 2024, Elon Musk outlined that the operating cost of a Cybercab is "probably going to be $0.20" per mile, with "The price of everything would be about $0.30 to $0.40 per mile," with a Cybercab cost of $30,000.

However, these are Tesla's costs, so any individual buying a Cybercab to operate it as a robotaxi needs to factor in the $299-per-month full self-driving (FSD) subscription fee. Assuming a Cybercab is moderately run for 300,000 miles, it could rack up four years of subscriptions worth $14,352 in FSD costs.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

By "everything," Musk presumably means the fully loaded cost per mile, which includes Cybercab cost, energy cost, maintenance, cleaning, remote operations, and any other operational costs, in the TCO per-mile target of $0.30.

It has been revealed that this is where the battle over robotaxis will be won, because Tesla is highly likely to face competition from rivals developing low-cost electric vehicles (EVs) equipped with autonomous driving software. While its vision-only approach, leadership in EVs, scaling of Cybercab, and lead in the operational learning that will reduce TCO per mile give it a massive initial edge, it does not mean its robotaxi margins can't be eroded over time.

To illustrate this, consider the following scenario: a Cybercab costing $30,000, with a useful life of 300,000 miles, compared with a low-cost EV robotaxi costing $20,000, with a useful life of 400,000 miles:.

The argument that bears often use against Tesla is that rivals could eat into its competitive advantage, but I think it's flawed.

In a recent development, first, Tesla's vision-only approach implies lower structural hardware costs than the light detection and ranging (LiDAR) systems used by Waymo and others. Second, autonomous driving software is not free, and robotaxis need to be purposely built for it, both of which add costs for Tesla's rivals.

In a recent development, third, assuming that rivals could even get to $0.20-per-mile operating costs (or another figure close to where Tesla will get) assumes they can build scale and operational learning that Tesla is doing now. Finally, rivals could go for higher hardware costs (LiDAR plus licensed software) and more miles of robotaxi operation, but that would mean higher up-front costs, probably more maintenance costs, and robotaxis becoming obsolete more swiftly.

It has been revealed that the good news is that Tesla's miles under robotaxi expansion mean it's learning to reduce TCO per mile before others can. That's a massive edge.

FT, NYT tie Alice Huang’s chip network to gaming tycoons and PLA suppliers

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California.
  • Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday.
  • TNW has not independently verified either report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California.

Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday. Together they formed a network that supplied Nvidia chips to China. A day earlier, The Upcoming York Times tied companies linked to her family to suppliers of China’s military.

TNW has not independently verified either report. US officials suspect Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, the Times first reported in October, describing a Chinese spy plot. Beijing calls the claim a smear. Jensen Huang quit as Nvidia’s chief executive on 12 November after admitting an affair with her. They are not related.

In a recent development, the FT’s Zijing Wu and Haohsiang Ko traced the Alice Huang chip network through hundreds of filings and more than a dozen sources. Its companies made billions moving Nvidia chips into China, not necessarily aware of the full picture, the paper reported.

According to recent reports, it started with Inspur, one of Nvidia’s largest server partners in China. The US put Inspur on its entity list in March 2023, but not its part-owned US unit. Renamed Aivres, that unit kept trading with Nvidia. Inside Nvidia there were questions over whether it should count as a partner, a person with direct knowledge told the FT. Nvidia concluded that it met all compliance and export control rules.

Industry observers note that some of Inspur’s Chinese clients then turned to Century Huatong, an online gaming group turned data centre investor. The answer, people familiar with the plan mentioned, was an offshore shell branded as a “neocloud”. That shell became Megaspeed, with Huang as its trusted public face.

Kang Wei, whom the FT calls her husband and the Times her business partner, was an early investor in Century Huatong, filings show. Megaspeed grew out of the Singapore arm of 7Road, a gaming firm that Huang and Century Huatong both backed. Its Malaysian unit, Speedmatrix, declared about $4.6bn of imports from Aivres in the year to December 2025. The FT cites ImportGenius trade data.

It has been revealed that the last step was smuggling the chips into China. Hu Xiaowei filled at least part of that role, people familiar with the matter told the FT. US authorities call Hu the “second-in-command” at Prince Group. The US Treasury has named the group a transnational criminal organisation. Hu was arrested in Japan this summer.

A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu never worked for the business and called the US allegations unsupported. The FT could not reach Hu.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia said it put Megaspeed and a subsidiary on its block list in 2025 and has also restricted sales to Aivres. Megaspeed has said it runs a lawful business, and that Huang left in August 2025. Tencent, which owns 10.1% of Century Huatong, said it knew nothing of the activities. The FT found no evidence that Tencent or Alibaba took part.

Industry observers note that the Times reviewed a confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an intelligence firm staffed by former intelligence officers. About $3.6bn of Chinese state money flowed through companies tied to Huang’s family or associates, it found. The money funded projects including data centres with Nvidia chips. The Times said it confirmed many of the ties itself.

Most links are indirect, the Times said, and it is unclear whether the military used any of the computing power. The paper had already reported that Megaspeed’s backer Alibaba co-founded a military-linked lab.

“Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it,” Strider’s chief executive, Greg Levesque, told the Times.

Industry observers note that both papers point to Century Litong, a Shanghai firm founded by Century Longteng. The FT says Longteng was a venture between Century Huatong and a vehicle Huang controlled with her sister. The Times names the sister’s firm.

In a recent development, century Litong was a key distributor of smuggled Nvidia chips in China, people with knowledge of the deals told the FT. The Information first reported its role. Its owner, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, also controls a maker of Chinese radar and missile parts, the Times reported.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to Century Litong’s Hong Kong unit, licence files released on Thursday by a House committee show. An Nvidia spokesman told the Times that, despite receiving some licences, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and had not and would not ship to that firm. Century Litong notes it has no dealings with Huang. Nvidia’s shares, meanwhile, have had their worst run since 2008.

It's not just the semiconductor industry that's under pressure. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) is officially in a correction -- a decline of at least 10% from its high.

According to recent reports, as tempting as it may be to scoop up beaten-down semiconductor ETFs, the Vanguard Morningstar Mega Cap Growth ETF (MGK -5.58%) could be an even better growth ETF for long-term AI stock investors. Here's why.

Investors likely gravitate toward SOXX and DRAM for their outsize weightings in top semiconductor stocks. As of Nov. 13, SOXX had a combined 38.9% weighting in just five stocks -- Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -13.25%), Broadcom (AVGO -12.19%), Micron Technology (MU -13.89%), Nvidia, and Intel (INTC -7.97%). DRAM is far more concentrated, with a 28.1% weighting in Samsung Electronics (SSNLF +0.00%) , 27.2% in Micron, and 22% in SK Hynix (SKHY -13.11%) as of Nov. 16.

The Vanguard Morningstar Mega Cap Growth ETF is also centered around a handful of leading companies. But the key difference is that these companies span all stock market sectors, not just the semiconductor industry. As of Oct. 31, Apple (AAPL -1.90%) is the largest holding at 13.8% of the ETF, followed by Nvidia at 13.1%, Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) at 10.3%, and Alphabet (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%) at 7.8%.

Investors who are curious about the semiconductor-specific exposure in MGK can note that Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, Applied Materials (AMAT -10.71%), Lam Research (LRCX -10.02%), Intel, KLA (KLAC -10.33%), Marvell Technology (MRVL -11.69%), Sandisk (SNDK -16.05%), Seagate Technology (STX -12.35%), and Western Digital (WDC -12.02%) make up a combined 27.1% of the fund -- giving it significant pure-play exposure to the industry.

The fund gives investors significantly more tech exposure than an S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) index fund. And it's a more concentrated bet on a handful of names than the Vanguard Growth ETF (VUG -5.32%), which is more diversified, with 135 holdings compared to 52 for MGK. But MGK isn't solely invested in major tech-focused companies. Healthcare giant Eli Lilly (LLY -0.30%) makes up 4.1% of the ETF. Visa (V -0.09%) and Mastercard (MA -0.14%) are 2.3% and 1.8%, respectively.

SOXX and DRAM invest in AI stocks purely through a semiconductor lens, whereas MGK offers a far better long-term investment that should ultimately prove less cyclical and less dependent on a single theme. For example, Apple remains just a few percentage points off its all-time high because the organization doesn't depend on high capital expenditures to invest in AI over the long term. Instead, its products and services are the touchpoint between people and AI applications and tools.

Microsoft, Amazon (AMZN -4.10%), and Alphabet are heavily invested in AI infrastructure through their data center build-outs. But they also have exposure to other segments of the AI value chain through services and enterprise software application layers, and consumer electronics. Additionally, Alphabet has its own leading model in Gemini. And Amazon could become one of the largest owners of edge AI through robotic warehouse automation.

Industry observers note that eli Lilly should enjoy significant cost-reduction benefits from AI, which could allow it to accelerate drug development. There's also a slew of software companies in MGK that hyperscalers ultimately depend on to buy cloud capacity. And as the companies behind leading frontier models go public, MGK will likely gradually accumulate shares, whereas SOXX and DRAM won't, as they aren't classified as chip stocks.

Recent findings suggest that SOXX and DRAM shine when customers are lining up to buy cutting-edge logic and memory chips. And there are plenty of reasons to believe that many top chip stocks remain solid buys now. But the semiconductor industry can be cyclical. And there will likely come a time when most of the growth along the AI value chain occurs downstream of pick-and-shovel plays in companies developing useful AI-powered tools and applications.

According to recent reports, it's also worth mentioning that SOXX and DRAM have more expensive fee structures than MGK. SOXX charges a 0.33% expense ratio, and DRAM's is even higher at 0.65%. MGK charges a dirt cheap 0.05% expense ratio, or just $0.50 for every $1,000 invested.

Add it all up, and MGK is a better long-term buy for investors seeking leading growth stocks that could benefit from AI in a variety of ways, rather than solely betting on the infrastructure layer via semiconductor stocks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic logo, Guilherand-Granges, France, March 2025.
  • According to recent reports, mmathematician at Anthropic says he has used the company’s Claude AI model to prove the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics.
  • “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic logo, Guilherand-Granges, France, March 2025.

According to recent reports, mmathematician at Anthropic says he has used the company’s Claude AI model to prove the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge made the claim in a note on his website on Friday, Bloomberg reported.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote.

Industry observers note that the hypothesis, first proposed in 1859, concerns how prime numbers are spread out. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which carries a $1m prize. Alpöge says his proof also covers a broader version, the generalised Riemann hypothesis.

It has been revealed that he did not publish a traditional paper. Instead, he released the proof in Lean, a programming language that checks every logical step. The code runs to about 17 million lines, Science reported.

Andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at MIT, told Bloomberg he had checked the code on his own computer. He remarked he had seen at least three other checks by professional mathematicians. Later on Friday, Sutherland put the chance that anything is wrong at roughly zero, Scientific American reported.

However, other mathematicians urged caution. A proof that compiles in Lean still has to state the right problem, and humans have to confirm that it does.

It has been revealed that kevin Buzzard, a professor at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof shows, Al Jazeera reported. The proof has not been formally accepted.

Alpöge noted Claude did much of the work.

“This time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, anthropic declined to comment to Bloomberg. The claim came a day after the firm’s record stock market debut.

According to recent reports, if confirmed, it would be the second Millennium Prize Problem that AI may have helped solve. In September, OpenAI said its models had produced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Matt Frankel, CFP® – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:18AM EST.
  • In a recent development, in January, one notable firm told its investors that Anthropic could be worth about $2 trillion by 2030.
  • The stock gave back a good chunk of its first-day gains, but even at about $96 as of this writing, Anthropic is worth about $1.7 trillion on a fully diluted basis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Frankel, CFP® – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:18AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

In a recent development, in January, one notable firm told its investors that Anthropic could be worth about $2 trillion by 2030. On Thursday, Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) hit that valuation in its very first trade as a public firm, roughly four years ahead of schedule.

The stock gave back a good chunk of its first-day gains, but even at about $96 as of this writing, Anthropic is worth about $1.7 trillion on a fully diluted basis. That already puts it among the world's largest companies, but I think it can go much further. In fact, I predict that by the end of 2030, Anthropic will be the most valuable company on the planet.

Apple (AAPL -1.90%) is presently the world's most valuable tech giant, worth about $5.2 trillion as of Nov. 13. Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) was worth more than $5 trillion as recently as early November, but a six-week slide has pushed it below $3.6 trillion.

It has been revealed that of course, the bar will keep rising. While we don't know what Apple's stock price will do, if the tech giant grows its market value by about 8% a year, it would be worth roughly $7 trillion by the end of 2030. A rebound in Nvidia could push the top spot even higher. A realistic estimate is that Anthropic would need to be worth somewhere between $7 trillion and $10 trillion to claim first place, about four to six times its current value. I'm well aware that this is a bold prediction. But I think it's within the realm of possibilities.

Anthropic's third-quarter revenue was $17.0 billion, up 1,127% from a year earlier. As of the latest information, the company revealed that its annual revenue run rate had surpassed $80 billion.

In a recent development, if revenue grows by about 50% a year from here, Anthropic would generate roughly $340 billion of annual revenue by 2030. At 20 to 25 times sales, which is about where the stock trades today, the organization would be worth about $7 trillion to $8.5 trillion. Growth of 50% per year would be a dramatic slowdown from Anthropic's current pace, and, quite frankly, I think this scenario is more realistic than a best-case.

Here's why. The average Fortune 500 customer right now allocates less than 0.1% of its spending to Anthropic's Claude tools. But it's clear that people are finding tremendous value, and the company's net revenue retention rate of 900% means that the average existing customer now spends nine times as much as they did a year ago. Anthropic could grow its average revenue per customer by a further 10x multiple and still account for less than 1% of its customers' overall spending. As AI evolves and Claude tools become more essential to the day-to-day operations of Anthropic's enterprise clients, this is certainly possible.

It's not only top-line growth that could propel the stock higher. It's that Anthropic is becoming more profitable over time, and this is likely to continue as the business scales and compute and infrastructure costs (as a percentage of revenue) decline.

Recent findings suggest that over the past few years, most of the profits from the AI boom have gone to the companies selling the hardware, such as Nvidia. I expect more of that value to shift toward the companies with the best AI models over time, and I'm not alone. Atreides Management founder Gavin Baker has argued that Anthropic could eventually pass Nvidia as the world's most valuable company for this reason. In a nutshell, Nvidia sells the picks and shovels of the AI boom, while Anthropic is building the mine itself. https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/upcoming-ipo-could-soon-surpass-160226425.html.

Industry observers note that it's also worth noting that Anthropic has powerful partners. Amazon (AMZN -4.10%) and Alphabet (GOOGL -2.70%)(GOOG -2.59%), two of its biggest customers, will own nearly 15% and 14% of the company, respectively, after the IPO.

As I mentioned earlier, this is a bold call, and there are several reasons why I could be wrong. Competition from Anthropic's rivals, including OpenAI and Alphabet's Google, is intense, and AI model prices could fall faster than usage grows. Anthropic is also spending enormous sums. It posted a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter and has about $900 billion of computing and infrastructure commitments. And Apple and Nvidia are hardly standing still when it comes to their own innovation.

As a CFP, I'd also add that a bold prediction isn't a reason to bet the farm. I'm planning to build an Anthropic stock position gradually, and I'd keep any young, volatile stock to a modest share of a portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that having said all that, if Anthropic keeps growing at even a fraction of its current pace, I think the market will eventually value the company building the AI models more than the companies supplying the chips and devices. This is a five-year call, not a price target for next week, but I wouldn't be at all surprised to see Anthropic sit at the top of the market-cap rankings by the end of 2030.

Among iOS 27’s many new features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces significant AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting new features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the patch also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

After iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most consumers will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

Industry observers note that I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple prepares to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Taiwan widens its short-selling ban after the Taiex’s worst week since 1991

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (309 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Taiwan’s financial regulator has banned all short selling of local stocks below the previous day’s closing price.
  • Short selling is a bet that a share price will fall.
  • The FSC also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taiwan’s financial regulator has banned all short selling of local stocks below the previous day’s closing price. The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) announced the move on Saturday, Bloomberg reported. It takes effect on 23 November.

Short selling is a bet that a share price will fall. The ban covers both margin short sales and sales of borrowed shares. Securities and futures firms that short stocks to hedge their business are exempt.

The FSC also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130%. In addition, it stopped taking applications from brokers to list latest put warrants, which also pay out when prices fall.

It is the third round of short-selling curbs this month. On 9 November, the FSC cut the cap on intraday short sales of borrowed shares from 30% to 3% of average daily volume, Crowdfund Insider reported.

A second round on 19 November banned shorting below the previous close for stocks that fell at least 3.5% the day before, according to Focus Taiwan.

Neither round stopped the slide. The Taiex fell 6.2% on Friday and lost almost 18% over the week, its worst week since 1991, according to Bloomberg. Doubts about whether AI spending will pay off have hit tech shares across Asia.

Meanwhile, Taiwan’s NT$500bn ($15bn) National Financial Stabilization Fund noted it has been buying shares since 6 November. The fund said worries about tighter US regulation of AI, returns on massive capital spending and margin-financing risks had triggered the sell-off.

Taiwan’s finance ministry remarked the economy remains strong. It grew 14.4% in the third quarter, and October export orders rose 78% from a year earlier, Bloomberg reported.

Tech Report: Johnson & Johnson Is on Track for $101 Billion in 2026 Sales. Is This Dividend King Still a Buy?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:38AM EST.
  • Johnson & Johnson (JNJ +1.25%) is the kind of investment that you buy and hold for the long term.
  • Industry observers note that it is vital to understand that Johnson & Johnson has an incredible business history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:38AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Johnson & Johnson ›.

Johnson & Johnson (JNJ +1.25%) is the kind of investment that you buy and hold for the long term. However, that doesn't mean it will be a great option for every investor. While it could be a buy for a conservative dividend investor today, many others will likely be better off putting the stock on their wish list. Here's why.

Industry observers note that it is vital to understand that Johnson & Johnson has an incredible business history. Founded more than 100 years ago, the business has proven resilient, changing over time to serve its customers and reward its shareholders. Today, the manufacturer is an industry leader in both the pharmaceutical and medical devices segments of the broader healthcare sector.

There are many ways that J&J's success could be highlighted, but one of the best is probably its dividend track record. The healthcare giant has increased its dividend for 64 consecutive years. That not only makes J&J a Dividend King but also gives it the longest streak of any healthcare company. A company can't build a dividend track record like that by accident; it requires a strong business model that gets executed well in good times and bad.

Recent findings suggest that during the third quarter, J&J again indicated how well it is run, increasing its full-year guidance for revenues and earnings. On the top line, the healthcare behemoth now projects $101.2 billion in revenue, with the bottom line at $11.10 per share. Those are both modest improvements over the previous guidance, but the direction is what's important. If you own this stock, you should be pleased with the third-quarter 2026 update.

In a recent development, the problem is that Wall Street knows that J&J is a well-run organization. That's why the yield is 1.9%, above the market's tiny 1% and the average healthcare stock's 1.3%, but still unlikely to be enticing to investors looking to maximize the income their portfolios generate. The yield is also near its lowest levels in the past decade. That speaks to another problem: valuation.

Industry observers note that johnson & Johnson's price-to-sales ratio is 6.8x compared to a five-year average of 4.8x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is 42x, compared with a long-term average of 24x. And its price-to-book ratio is 8.2x versus a five-year average of 5.8x. While the P/E ratio has been biased higher by one-time charges, the overall statement here is that J&J is expensive. So value investors will probably want to stay on the sidelines.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Industry observers note that there is, however, a place for Johnson & Johnson if you are a conservative, income-oriented investor who places a high value on dividend consistency. This is, basically, a situation where investors are paying up for quality. That said, if you are patient, you could probably buy the stock with a more attractive yield and valuation during a broad market downturn. So even here, it could be a wish-list stock. But if you are looking to buy a diversified healthcare stock that you can count on for the long term, it deserves strong consideration despite the premium price tag.

It would be wonderful if great companies were also cheap and had above-average dividend yields. That's just not how Wall Street works most of the time. If you have a value focus or favor high-yield stocks, J&J probably won't fit your portfolio right now. Keep it on your wish list, just in case a market downdraft opens up a buying opportunity. However, if what you are looking for is a reliable dividend stock with an above-market yield, paying a premium for J&J could still be worth it if you have a long enough time horizon.

Latest Update: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Recent findings suggest that data centers already use light in networking.
  • In a recent development, the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Recent findings suggest that data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

In a recent development, the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” states Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

In a recent development, optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Industry observers note that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The manufacturer’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

In a recent development, “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” states Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Upcoming Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Recent findings suggest that back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon states this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also crucial to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the tech giant’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is at the moment choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.
