#62451. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4731 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

In a recent development, many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon revealed his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Sources indicate that amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is notable because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

In a recent development, I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

In a recent development, such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

McKibillo The Game of Superintelligence  How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might leadKey • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress1. Alan Turing1936Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.REALITY CHECK Reveals that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm.2. I. J. Good1965Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”3. Backpropagation1986Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.4. Vernor Vinge1993Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”REALITY CHECK Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess.5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky1990s–2000sBostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.6. Deep learning breakthroughs 2010sLarger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.7. The race to self-improving AI2020sDario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.8. Reality check 2020sFrançois Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.YOU ARE HERE2026AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES1. The Intelligence ExplosionAI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.2. Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead.

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision.

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development.

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress.

Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

According to recent reports, claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

According to recent reports, an intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Sources indicate that finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Industry observers note that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

Industry observers note that there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

Industry observers note that but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s key to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Recent findings suggest that last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

It has been revealed that in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Recent findings suggest that though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

Industry observers note that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

It has been revealed that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Industry observers note that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the firm judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

Also: 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers.

In a recent development, apple hasn’t been shy about stating that the use of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence for specific tasks would face daily access limits. Increased limits would be granted based on your iCloud+ subscription. Now the company has revealed how much it will cost you and when the limits will begin.

Industry observers note that “Starting with the 2027 software releases, Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are available for free for customers with a supported device set to a supported language,” Apple said on a support page updated November 16. “Some features rely on powerful server models and have limits where increased access is available with eligible iCloud+ plans, starting with the 27.3 release.”.

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in early December, so that’s when the daily usage limits will kick in.

At that point, people with no paid iCloud+ plan and even those with the $0.99-per-month 50 GB plan will be the most limited, with Apple saying only that they’ll face a “Standard Device Limit.”.

In a recent development, what is a standard limit? That depends not just on how many times you tap into Siri per day but on what tasks you assign it. Basic Siri commands, such as setting timers and alarms or sending standard text messages, will remain free and unlimited.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster.

Advanced Siri and Apple Intelligence tasks will bump into the usage limits. These include the following, according to Apple:.

Sources indicate that one positive here is that the limits are per device not per account. That means you can use Siri AI and Apple Intelligence with the same account across your iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro without fear of chewing up too much of your quota.

This all sounds like a way for Apple to steer people to more expensive iCloud+ accounts. But the limits are in place for a key reason. Basic commands are processed on your device, so they don’t require the use of Apple servers. More advanced tasks are processed using server-side AI models, which can feel the strain if too many people access them all at once.

Also: What you’ll pay for AI agents will be wildly variable and unpredictable.

Industry observers note that how will you know if you use up your daily allotment and what happens then? You’ll receive a notification if you hit your limit for a particular feature category. At that point, you can still give Siri basic tasks to perform. But advanced ones will be paused until your limit resets the next day. Otherwise, Apple is undoubtedly hoping that people who continually run into limits will upgrade to a pricier iCloud+ blueprint.

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 22, 2026 at 9:30AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

According to recent reports, nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) was the world's most valuable company a month ago. Now, its valuation has been cut in half.

The stock plunged 23% last week, its worst week since the height of the financial crisis in 2008, as the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation continues to play out.

In the midst of Nvidia's plunge, the AI chip leader reported another blowout earnings report, posting 103% revenue growth in the third quarter with strong margins, and it raised its guidance for next year.

The report was a reminder that even as the company is in turmoil over its leadership and multiple investigations over its chip exports to China, the business is as strong as ever, and some investors see the sell-off as a buying opportunity.

Nvidia is now cheaper than it's ever been, trading at a forward P/E of just 8, and it just doubled its revenue. Typically, a stock growing that fast is valued at such a low multiple because investors don't expect those profits to last.

In Nvidia's case, that could be for two reasons. First, the semiconductor sector is cyclical, and Nvidia has gone through several market cycles before. The AI infrastructure build-out will eventually peak, which could lead to Nvidia's sales peaking in the AI boom. The four major hyperscalers are planning to spend $700 billion on capital expenditures this year, and cash flow has turned negative for some of them, meaning that level of spending isn't sustainable.

The other explanation for Nvidia's low P/E ratio is that investors are skeptical of the firm's long-term growth after Huang's resignation and as the company faces investigations and potential consequences like fines, tighter export restrictions, and increased oversight after Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence agent who was helping to funnel Nvidia chips to China.

According to recent reports, no one knows the outcome of these investigations, and Nvidia's next permanent CEO remains a question mark as well. The bad news isn't necessarily over for Nvidia. On Friday, Reuters reported that the SEC is investigating the manufacturer over accounting challenges, which contributed to a 14% drop in the stock.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia faces an extraordinary number of risks right now. The only CEO the organization has had in its 33 years is gone, and he exercised an unusual degree of control over the company and its relationships with customers and suppliers, including spinning a complex web of financing to help backstop the AI sector. Additionally, Congress and several government agencies are investigating the company over chip export violations.

On the other hand, Nvidia shares are incredibly cheap, down by nearly 50% from their peak last month, and if the manufacturer can overcome the challenges it at the moment faces, it looks like a surefire winner. Just getting back to where it was in October would be a double, and the company continues to dominate the market for AI chips, as its recent earnings report indicates.

Industry observers note that my honest take, though, is that there are easier opportunities to take advantage of the AI sell-off from stocks that don't have the risks that Nvidia does. TSMC, for example, is down 35% from its peak last month, and the world's largest chip manufacturer has one of the widest economic moats in business. Alphabet and Meta Platforms aren't as directly exposed to AI as Nvidia, but both trade at P/Es below 20, and they're down by roughly a third from their peaks this year.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

If you recognize the risk and volatility facing Nvidia and still want to buy it, I think the best way to do so is with a variation of the dollar-cost averaging method.

I would choose a target amount I was willing to invest, capped at 5% of my portfolio,and invest a quarter now at $125, and then invest another quarter each time the stock falls 10%, if that happens. So, I'd invest another quarter of the allotment at $112, the next quarter at $101, and the last at $91. This method allows you to take advantage of further pullbacks, which we could see given the uncertainty facing the company.

If you exercised all of those purchases, you'd have a cost basis of $107 on Nvidia, and if the stock doesn't fall that far, you'd still benefit.

Industry observers note that over the long term, I think Nvidia is more likely than not to recover, but that could take years, and we’re likely to see considerable volatility over the coming months. If you're interested in the stock, saving some cash to take advantage of deeper sell-offs makes sense.

According to recent reports, even if you haven’t played a video game since Frogger, it’s tough to ignore Thursday’s launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, the most preordered video game of all time. Some companies gave employees a day off to play. (CNET bosses, I’d like the same for the next Animal Crossing game, OK?).

Recent findings suggest that mcDonald’s rolled out a promotion that lets GTA 6 players order burgers and fries via Discord without stopping the game. And CNET’s Andrew Lanxon played it for 24 hours straight at his Edinburgh home, much to his ignored cat’s dismay.

Sources indicate that naturally, the memes and jokes are revved up. I’ve never played any of the Grand Theft Autos, and I still laughed at these.

Many of the memes play off a common complaint about how long it took the much-anticipated GTA 6 to arrive: 13 years.

“We got [fill in the blank] before GTA 6” was the usual caption.

We deadass got a whole upcoming ocean before GTA 6 https://t.co/dE9MVty8js.

The Marvel Mania account went one step further and listed as many things as possible that “we got” before GTA 6, including COVID-19, a new English king, foldable phones, a second Donald Trump presidency, an American pope, McDonald’s Grimace shake, the Hawk Tuah meme, the Roman Empire trend and many more.

Industry observers note that people immediately started looking for a fresh long-awaited item to fill GTA 6’s place in the meme. George R.R. Martin’s eternal Game of Thrones sequel, yer up!

Now it just goes back to "We got ______ before George RR Martin's THE WINDS OF WINTER".

It has been revealed that GTA 6 might be fun for players, but not for the fictional cops in the game. Minnesota’s South St. Paul Police Department was one of several actual law-enforcement agencies that got in on the release hype, posting: “Our thoughts are with the Vice City Police Department tonight as they prepare for an influx of visitors.”.

According to recent reports, GTA 6 includes 34 types of cats and dogs you can pet, as well as other animals. If you spend any time on social media, you know cats are a favorite pick. This post jokes about coaxing the little furballs with the “pspsps” sounds.

According to recent reports, sure, you can do wild, crazy things in GTA 6, but you can also… grocery shop? Numerous memes have poked fun at a screenshot noting that Lucia “will appreciate” it if you bring home groceries.

Wrote one Bluesky user, “I think I’m going to spend all my time in GTA6 fixing up the house, buying groceries, raiding gang hideouts, feeding my pet. Total escapism from life where I can barely afford any of that.”.

Recent findings suggest that I think I’m going to spend all my time in GTA6 fixing up the house, buying groceries, raiding gang hide outs, feeding my pet. Total escapism from life where I can barely afford any of that.

Apparently, you can also pull a Tom Sawyer’s pals and do a little painting.

“GTA only promotes violence and crime”Me playing GTA 6: pic.twitter.com/CYGjsZQD2W.

The American Heart Association got in on the release hype by telling veteran players they’re old.

In a recent development, “If you’ve played GTA on more than one console generation, it’s time to get your cholesterol checked,” one post read. Thanks a lot, Mom.

According to recent reports, if you're calling in sick to play GTA VI, you need to schedule your annual visit. pic.twitter.com/sxHAh7wvZs.

Some joked that Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia might not have had anything to do with extramarital affairs or backdoor business deals with China. Maybe he just wanted unlimited time to play GTA 6.

Jensen huang resign as CEO just 5 days before the launch GTA VI pic.twitter.com/0Nwo0soqky.

Bro prepared affair for 2 year built RTX 5090 just to play GTA 6 pic.twitter.com/m5AUi3KCUr.

Some players complained that you can’t actually commit “grand theft auto” in the game. In reality, you can steal most cars by carjacking drivers or breaking into standard vehicles — only keyless and luxury models require a Key Cloner. Still, the fact that you can’t effortlessly steal every car on sight sparked a wave of memes mocking the game for not living up to its name.

According to recent reports, the Burnt Peanut was running into some issues this morning at the beginning of GTA 6 lmao"wait it's locked?? it's not your car, you need to buy it? sir the name of the game is GRAND THEFT AUTO. i simply grand theft upon an AUTOMOBILE" pic.twitter.com/avSU71JgXP.

And many memes had a sad tinge, focusing on PC gamers who were left out of the GTA 6 launch. There’s still no release date for the game’s PC version.

PC players going to work on November 19th will be like pic.twitter.com/mEzrQASMFg.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Gemini can now turn your notes and other sources in your Gemini Notebook (previously called NotebookLM) into interactive pages or sites to help you better process complicated information.

Industry observers note that complete with flashcards, dashboards, and colorful panels, the sites make it easier to study and understand intricate concepts. I tested the feature, announced Tuesday, to see how efficient it is at creating a navigable site that is actually helpful and stays loyal to sources.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector in my tests.

Sources indicate that because Notebooks are built with the sources you provide, like textbooks, files, or notes, the sites are created with the data that is in your Gemini Notebook. Notebook has three tabs: Sources, Chat, and Studio. The site option is in the Studio tab, listed under what you can create.

If you’re taking a college class, you could put all the information you need to prepare for a test and use the interactive site as a study guide that you can share with others.

To test this, I gave Notebook the following prompt:.

“Make me a site that visually explains how cellular respiration works, breaking down each stage with interactive diagrams and self-check flashcards.”.

It has been revealed that since I’m not in a class that would give me those study materials, I gave Gemini online sources to use for this. Gemini cited the sources in my notebook, then spent a few minutes creating the interactive site. Gemini will give you a quick update when it’s done, including a summary of the source information as it pertains to your request and instructions on where to find the site.

Also: I checked Gemini’s newly introduced Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours.

According to recent reports, as promised, my cellular respiration notes were complete and organized on an interactive, visually appealing site that was easy to navigate. The coolest feature on the site was the flashcards, which you can hover over to see which ones you’ve studied.

Recent findings suggest that the interactive site feature is now available to Gemini Notebook owners and will soon come to the mobile app. As someone who knows very little about coding, I was pretty satisfied to see the information Gemini put together presented in explorable, easy-to-understand tabs on a site.

Uber Is Testing Rides for Kids With Qualified Drivers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (441 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Uber, the popular ridesharing app, is testing rides for kids.
  • The pilot program for Uber Kids starts in three US cities for a limited time: Austin, Texas; Nashville, Tennessee; and Madison, Wisconsin.
  • In a recent development, on the surface, it feels like a questionable proposition, given all the potential harms and dangers to young people traveling alone with a stranger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber, the popular ridesharing app, is testing rides for kids. Uber Kids will cater to youngsters ages 10 to 12, those awkward years before adolescence. The new program expands on the company’s other offering to underage passengers, Uber Teens, which debuted in 2023 and provides rides to teenagers ages 13 to 17 in select cities.

The pilot program for Uber Kids starts in three US cities for a limited time: Austin, Texas; Nashville, Tennessee; and Madison, Wisconsin. Its expansion will depend on how well it performs in those regions. If successful, Uber Kids could bring a whole new influx of customers to the app, specifically parents and families needing help getting their kids from point A to point B.

In a recent development, on the surface, it feels like a questionable proposition, given all the potential harms and dangers to young people traveling alone with a stranger. But it seems like Uber took those concerns into account. The rideshare app has added a slew of mandatory requirements for both approved guardians and qualified drivers.

First off, kids won’t simply be able to order a ride for themselves. The adult user must add the child to their family profile and complete an onboarding session covering the service’s safety features. They’ll also need to set up PIN verification for every trip. The parent or guardian must be present at the pickup location and provide the driver with a note containing the drop-off instructions.

Industry observers note that as any parent would likely wonder (myself included), what about the drivers? How are they vetted?

According to Uber, only the highest-rated drivers will be invited to take part in the program. They’ll need to pass thorough background checks and successfully complete an Uber Kids education curriculum. Moreover, they must agree to use live video streaming in their cars so that parents and guardians can watch the trip every step of the way.

It has been revealed that live videos of underage passengers bring up a bunch of potential red flags, but Uber states all recordings will be encrypted, and no driver will have access to the content. Furthermore, sensors and GPS data will track the ride if the trip is interrupted or veers off course.

In a recent development, uber could face a tough time recruiting drivers for Uber Kids. Transporting minors adds extra responsibility and requires specific skills that many drivers may want to avoid. To sweeten the deal, Uber is offering eligible drivers a $20 bonus on their first ride and an extra $7 per trip after that.

An Uber spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment.

By James Halley – Nov 22, 2026 at 9:53AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Gilead Sciences ›.

Gilead Sciences (GILD -0.06%) increased its dividend by 3.8% this year, the 11th consecutive year of dividend increases. Its dividend yield is above average, at 1.94%, based on the stock's current price.

According to recent reports, the organization holds a dominant position in HIV therapies, and these drugs provide dependable cash flow for the near future. Gilead is also seeing expansions into other areas, including oncology, liver, and inflammation therapies.

There are three reasons why Gilead's dividend is a safe bet to continue to grow.

Over nine months, Gilead produced $10.6 billion in free cash flow, up 68% year over year, leaving its cash dividend payout ratio at just below 30%. Spending less than a third of its cash flow on its dividend leaves this pharmaceutical company with plenty of funds to buy back stock, fund research and development, and increase its dividend.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

The manufacturer's lead drug, Biktarvy, brought in $4.1 billion in the third quarter, up 10% year over year. It commands a 53% U.S. market share and holds patent exclusivity through 2036.

In the meantime, its newer HIV therapies, such as Yeztugo and Descovy, are rapidly improving sales. Descovy revenue rose 49% year over year to $1 billion in the third quarter, and Yeztugo's sales jumped 682% from the same period a year ago to $305 million.

While HIV therapies remain its primary revenue source, the firm has worked hard to broaden its portfolio.

It has been revealed that breast cancer drug Trodelvy has become a blockbuster product, one of seven Gilead medications that bring in more than $1 billion a year. Trodelvy recently obtained European approval in combination with pembro to treat first-line PD-L1-positive metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. The therapy brought in $506 million in the third quarter, up 42% over the same period a year ago.

Gilead has seven clinical-stage antibody-drug conjugate oncology programs in the pipeline.

The company reported revenue of $203 million in the quarter for liver disease treatment Livdelzi, up 93% year over year. Gilead's pipeline includes 49 clinical programs, including more than a dozen inflammation and immunology candidates such as emvistegrast, which highlighted strong phase-2 response rates in ulcerative colitis.
